prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, from the magic-wavelength concept to systematic uncertainties at the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: After reading all eight opening ballots I move my preferred configuration from B009 to B061. Optical lattice clocks have the broadest and most robust support in the room: B061 is ranked by seven of eight members, first by Kroll and Lindroth, and in the top three by five. It is also the candidate on which the attribution problem is smallest. Katori's magic-wavelength lattice removes Doppler and recoil shifts, and Ye's group took strontium clocks to 10^-18 systematic uncertainty and the many-body clock regime, so two names cover the conceptual step and the decisive demonstration. Several independent laboratories now reproduce the performance, and clock comparisons over fibre and free-space links test it. The scientific payoff is already realised and ongoing in tests of relativistic redshift at millimetre scales, constraints on varying constants, and the basis for redefining the second. As an experimentalist I value that this is an instrument-driven advance whose consequences were measured, not only anticipated. B009 remains a field-opening observational discovery that I still rate very highly, but I now think it is the weaker prize configuration for this year.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is overlap with earlier metrology prizes: Hall and Hansch (2005, the frequency comb) and Wineland and Haroche (2012, control of single quantum systems, including ion clocks) can be read as having already honoured the clock revolution. Ion-clock pioneers and other lattice-clock groups (Lemonde, Ludlow, Takamoto, PTB, NIST, SYRTE) are outside the two credited names. Finally, the redefinition of the second has not yet happened, so a prize now rewards a demonstrated capability rather than a completed transition in practice.

responses.point: Ranked B061 first as a clean, concrete advance in measurement with stable interpretation and independent confirmation, while flagging a personal connection to the Hall laboratory tradition and noting that Wineland's 2012 prize is a partial precedent.
responses.response: I agree with the core assessment and the maturity argument. On the 2012 precedent I disagree that it weakens the case much: the Wineland and Haroche citation concerned measuring and manipulating individual quantum systems, whereas the lattice clock's novelty is interrogating a large ensemble of neutral atoms in a magic-wavelength trap, which is a different route to accuracy and a different set of systematics. I would ask that Kroll's disclosed Hall-lineage connection be noted in the record when his ranking is weighed, but it does not change my reading, because Lindroth, who has no such tie, reaches the same ranking independently.

responses.point: Ranked B061 first because the atomic-structure physics of the magic wavelength and blackbody-shift control is directly judgeable, and argued that the 2005 comb prize left the clock application unrecognised.
responses.response: This is the argument that most moved me. The magic wavelength depends on matching differential polarisabilities of the clock states, and control of the blackbody shift is what makes 10^-18 credible; a specialist in atomic structure confirming these are sound physics, not merely engineering, answers my own worry that I was judging this outside my field. I accept Lindroth's view that the comb prize enabled the clock but did not recognise the lattice-clock concept or its accuracy demonstration, though I note Lindroth flags the roles of PTB, NIST and SYRTE as an unresolved credit question that a two-name prize will not fully settle.

responses.point: Ranked B013 first (theory-plus-experiment, nature-delivered discovery, reproduced across moire platforms) and B009 third, noting that the credited names omit contributors such as Dean and that the source picture for the neutrinos is still evolving.
responses.response: I take his point that B013 is a discovery nature delivered and that independent reproduction is now broad, and I have revised my own earlier hesitation on maturity. I still hold two reservations: the experimental credit is delicate because Yuan Cao, the first author, and other experimental groups are outside the credited list, and the superconducting mechanism is unresolved. I would keep B013 as my first alternative rather than preferred. I also agree with his caution on B009: the observation that most of the diffuse flux has no identified source is a fair reason for me to move IceCube down from my opening first place.

responses.point: Ranked B013 first as a rare case where calculation anticipated a qualitatively new regime that experiment then confirmed, and suggested a MacDonald plus Jarillo-Herrero pairing could be an alternative to the three-name set.
responses.response: I find the prediction-then-observation structure persuasive and I agree a two-person MacDonald and Jarillo-Herrero configuration is defensible, since Bistritzer's share is the weakest link. My disagreement is about readiness relative to clocks: the interpretation of the correlated and superconducting states is still moving, whereas the lattice-clock claim is settled by repeated measurement. If the committee prefers a condensed-matter prize this year, B013 is where I would go, and I would favour the compact two-name version over the three-name one.

responses.point: Ranked B034 first, arguing the Cirac-Zoller proposals gave the conceptual blueprint for quantum information platforms and that the two-person theory configuration is clean, while acknowledging overlap with the 2012 prize.
responses.response: The attribution for Cirac and Zoller is indeed the cleanest of any candidate, and I do not dispute their influence. My reservation is that the 2012 prize recognised experiments on exactly the platforms their proposals targeted, and a theory-only award that bundles ion gates with cold-atom simulation has a blurred citation, which his own ballot notes. I therefore place it behind the lattice clock, where a single sharply defined achievement can be cited, but I would regard it as a serious option for a later year.

uncertainties: Whether the committee views lattice clocks as sufficiently distinct from the 2005 and 2012 metrology prizes to avoid an appearance of repetition.
Whether other lattice-clock groups and ion-clock pioneers should be reflected in the citation wording, since the statutes limit the prize to three people and only two names are credited.

I am relying on recollection of the technical history rather than verified sources, and my judgement of B009 may have been influenced by my own astroparticle background, so I defer to colleagues on the relative weight of B009 against B013.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile for B061, B013 or B009. My documented collaborations (PAMELA, Fermi-LAT, PoGOLite/PoGO+, XL-Calibur) do not include IceCube or the lattice-clock and moire communities, though B009 lies in my own field of astroparticle physics and I note that proximity when listing it as an alternative.
